newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr proves resilient to rate risks.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr proves resilient to rate risks.

text.p: The Australian dollar took advantage of yen weakness to push higher Monday, but could not completely shake off concerns the Reserve Bank will spring another rate cut on the market this week.

The main action came on the crosses where Japanese buying boosted the U.S. dollar to a 2-1/2 year high on the yen, lifting its Antipodean cousin above 88.00 yen in the process. Talk of demand linked to an A$ dual currency samurai also helped.
August current account data came in exactly as expected and continued a run of tolerable deficits which have all but anaesthetised investors to the trade problem.
By 4.45 pm (0645 GMT) the local dollar had crept cautiously ahead to US$0.7925/30 from an opening US$0.7906/11 and US$0.7923/28 late here Friday.

Minor support was seen at US$0.7880 with a more meaningful bulwark at last week's US$0.7855 low. Resistance had repeatedly proved formidable at US$0.7945 and there were further chart barriers US$0.7980 and 80 cents.

On the crosses it climbed to 88.24/34, not far short of a four year peak at 88.50, from 87.64/74 here Friday. In trade weighted terms it firmed to 58.5 from 58.4. The U.S. dollar shot to 111.33/38 yen from 110.82/87 late in New York Friday.

Traders warned the Australian currency needed a big yield buffer over the U.S. dollar to keep it attractive to Japanese investors and that would be in danger if the RBA board voted for another rate cut at its monthly meeting on Tuesday.

Falling domestic inflation and subdued jobs growth have convinced most analysts the central bank will ease rates again before year, probably after consumer price and wages data are released in late October. Some, however, saw no reason for the RBA to wait and would not be surprised if a cut came this week.
If the RBA did decide on an immediate easing it would likely come at its's money market operation on Wednesday morning.
If no move came then, the market would probably assume a cut was off the agenda until late October, dealers said.
Official cash rates currently stand at 7.0 percent having been cut by 0.50 point in a surprise move on July 31.

The bill market was already discounting such a reduction with the the December three month bank bill future at 93.41 implying a rate of 6.59 percent while the 10-year bond futures had surged to levels not seen since March 1994.
Today's current account data held few suprises, but exports did rise two percent to take the merchandise trade surplus to A$195 million, its highest level since February 1993.

The net income deficit, largely interest payments on foreign debt, remained by far the largest burden at A$1.638 billion and highlighted the need for long term efforts to cut the Australian budget deficit and build national savings.
More important for the course of monetary policy would be August retail trade and building approvals on Tuesday.
Sales are expected to fall 1.2 percent in August, unwinding some of the unbelievably strong 2.4 percent jump in July.
Indeed, so strong were they that many discounted them as a product of aberrant seasonal adjustment and deep discounting at stores desperate to clear shelves of old stock.
Some analysts were not so relaxed, noting that if prices were being cut sharply, then sale volumes must have really boomed to push the total value up by 2.4 percent.
This small group expect a flat to small rise in sales, which would point to a very strong contribution to Q3 GDP.
Building approvals are seen rising 1.0 percent in August after a hefty 8.1 percent gain in July, as strength in mortgage commitments slowly feeds through into the housing market.
Weakness in either would raise the chance of an early rate cut, but analysts noted a policy recommendation would have already been made to the RBA board.
